claims.text: High configurational entropy governs the structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
High configurational entropy thermodynamically stabilizes a single-phase solid solution.
High configurational entropy suppresses phase separation and chemical segregation.
The proposed starting nanoalloy is a homogeneous, near-equiatomic, single-phase solid solution.
The proposed thermal treatment spans approximately 800–1200°C in an inert atmosphere.
An inert or vacuum environment minimizes extrinsic chemical reactions during thermal exposure.
High configurational entropy enables retention of a disordered, single-phase solid-solution microstructure.
Configurational entropy lowers the free-energy difference between the homogeneous phase and potential segregated phases.
The entropy-associated free-energy change reduces the driving force for phase separation and chemical segregation at elevated temperature.
After high-temperature exposure, the high-entropy nanoalloy will retain a single-phase solid-solution structure with minimal chemical segregation.
Under the same thermal conditions, lower-configurational-entropy binary or ternary alloys will exhibit more phase separation than the high-entropy nanoalloy.
The prediction is limited to temperatures below the alloy melting point where diffusion is activated.
The prediction applies only when kinetic barriers do not override the proposed thermodynamic stabilization.
XRD can be used to assess phase-structure retention, and EDS can be used to assess chemical homogeneity.
Similar or greater phase separation and chemical segregation in the high-entropy nanoalloy relative to the lower-entropy control would falsify the hypothesis.
